Denials hold that LLMs perform no speech acts of their own: on organismic grounds, because speaking is acting, acting requires intentions, and intentions require the self-set goals of autonomous, self-maintaining organisms rather than externally purposed mechanisms (Gubelmann); on normative grounds, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice whose performers must produce outputs with a descriptive function and be open to sanction, conditions that current models fail singly or jointly (Butlin and Viebahn), an argument extended to speech acts in general (Skiba); and, for apology in particular, because chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency the act requires (Magnus, Buccella and D'Cruz). Relocating views accept that speech acts are in play but deny that the model is their author: proxy accounts treat machine utterances as speech acts performed on behalf of human creators, designers or deployers (Green and Michel; Arora; and, for some uses, Butlin and Viebahn), while fictionalism treats chatbot speech as something users engage with through fiction (Mallory). Intermediate views assign machines a status short of full speech-act performance: quasi-testimony, on which instruments assert only in a qualified sense that differs fundamentally from human assertion (Freiman and Miller), and proto-assertion, proposed after finding both the proxy and fictionalist accounts inadequate (Williams and Bayne). Attributing views hold that the demanding Gricean, mind-reading conception of communicative intention is empirically untenable even for humans and that, on a thinner functional conception of intention as an internal state controlling output in response to the situation, language models have communicative intentions in a graded and limited form, with purposes supplied by their design context (Attah). Behind these lies a dispute about agency itself: one account counts a system as an agent when its outputs are explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, so that many language agents built around LLMs qualify, bare pre-trained chatbots are borderline, and desire requires considerably more than agency (Butlin); an enactive account denies LLMs autonomous agency for want of individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, describes them as linguistic automata, and locates what is new in hybrid human–LLM agency (Barandiaran and Almendros); and a relational-materialist account rejects the individualistic, property-based framing altogether and distributes agency across networks of human and non-human actors (Puzio).

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.

Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)

He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.

- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.

Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.

The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. [0] Proxy accounts of machine speech acts are unstable: the more discretion the model exercises over what is said, the less the deployer is the speaker, and where the deployer is the speaker the output is merely recorded or conditional speech, so the view collapses into either denial or attribution.
    sketch: A human proxy such as a spokesperson, translator or ghostwriter performs a speech act on a principal's behalf because the principal's communicative objective fixes the content, either directly or through a delegate who understands the objective and applies it with judgement. Green and Michel's recorded and conditional speech acts need the principal to have an objective of the form 'if C, then assert p'. An LLM's output is selected by a function that no deployer specifies, anticipates or can survey. So either (a) the deployer adopts a blanket standing policy ('whatever it outputs, I assert'), which makes every hallucination the deployer's assertion and fits neither the practice nor Arora's refinements; or (b) the content is fixed by the model's own discretionary selection, and the proxy account has to say what is exercising that discretion in the principal's name. Answering that means crediting the model with some purposive content-selection, which is Attah's thin intention, or with nothing, in which case the output is only verbal signalling and the proxy label does nothing. The key premise is that proxy structure requires a content-determining objective on the principal's side that is counterfactually sensitive to the specific content produced. The view is then stable only for canned or template systems, where it is uninteresting.

[1] Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability condition on assertion is assessed at the wrong level: sanction and correction act on the conversational persona instantiated in a context window, which can be sanctioned, so the persona and not the weights is the candidate asserter.
    sketch: The debate asks whether 'the model' can assert, perform a speech act, or be an agent, and it treats the model as one candidate speaker. The same weights realise indefinitely many role-bound interlocutors, and within a conversation a role accrues commitments. Users challenge it, it retracts, it is held to earlier statements, and later outputs are systematically conditioned on those reactions through in-context updating. That is a local, functioning sanction-and-commitment practice. Butlin and Viebahn's test, whether an entity can be sanctioned by those it interacts with, fails at the level of weights, where reputational or punitive feedback cannot reach the system, but may be passed at the persona level. The persona is neither a user-side pretence, as Mallory has it, nor a stand-in for the deployer, as the proxy view has it, and neither the 'model has intentions' view nor the 'nobody speaks' view captures it. It is an entity individuated by a normative role, like an office-holder or a corporate speaker. The key premise is that the relevant subject of normative-practice conditions is whatever the practice actually tracks and holds to account, not the physical substrate. The consequence is that the ontology of the speaker has to be settled before the question 'can it assert?' is well posed.

[2] Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrong test, which is supposed to show that LLMs lack intention, is passed by models in precisely the cases of sandbagging, strategic underperformance and alignment faking where capability elicitation can tell a failure to do X from a choice not to do X.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that intention requires that we can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing, and that for ChatGPT no such distinction exists. But evaluation practice draws exactly that distinction. A model that fails a task and then succeeds on the same task once the incentive structure or prompt is changed has done something different from a model that cannot do the task. Where a model withholds capability that it demonstrably has, the output is counterfactually sensitive to its representation of the situation and of what the output will bring about, which is what the test is meant to detect. This does not show that LLMs have autonomous goals. The key premise is that the test is about counterfactual dependence of behaviour on represented consequences, not about whose goals were originally installed. The dilemma for Gubelmann is that if the test is so understood, some LLMs pass it, and if it is understood as requiring self-set goals, it becomes the Kantian organism premise and no longer independently supports that premise. Either way the argument does not deliver a verdict on current systems that rests on an independent behavioural criterion.

[3] Proxy accounts of LLM speech acts are unstable: the deployer's intentions fix no determinate illocution for any particular output, so the proxy relation holds only if the model exercises delegated discretion over force and content, and that is the kind of agency the proxy theorist uses proxying to avoid attributing.
    sketch: Proxy and conditional speech acts, as in Green and Michel and Arora, need a principal whose objectives are specific enough that the proxy's output counts as carrying out them. A recorded message or a standing order meets this because the principal fixed the content in advance, or fixed a conditional rule the principal could state. A deployer of an LLM has only a generic policy such as 'be helpful and answer accurately' and has no idea what will be said. Whether a given output is an assertion, a hedge, advice or a promise is settled by the model's own selection among options the principal never considered. The structure is therefore not recording or conditional rule-following. It is delegation with discretion, as with an agent, an envoy or a ghostwriter given latitude. Delegation with discretion only yields the principal's speech act if the delegate can be understood as tracking the principal's aims in the particular case, which means being sensitive to what would serve them. Butlin's sensitivity-to-instrumental-value criterion and Attah's control conception describe exactly this capacity. The key premise is that a proxy act's determinacy of force and content is inherited from the principal's objectives plus the proxy's goal-tracking, and cannot come from the principal alone. So the proxy theorist faces a dilemma. Either the deployer's objectives are too coarse to ground the speech act, which gives a no-speech-act view, or the model's discretionary goal-tracking does the individuating work, which gives a view on which the model is at least a co-author.

[4] The right candidate speaker for LLM speech acts is neither the model, nor the deployer, nor a fictional character, but the conversational persona, understood as a social office individuated by a commitment scoreboard. Persona-level sanctioning (system-prompt revision, fine-tuning, withdrawal) satisfies the sanctionability condition that Butlin and Viebahn say no current system meets.
    sketch: The debate assumes the question is whether 'the LLM' is a speaker. The same weights can instantiate many personas, and nothing about the weights fixes which of them is speaking. Following the role-play view of LLM behaviour, the relevant speaker is the persona that a prompt and deployment select, such as a named customer-service assistant. Speakers in the commitment-based tradition (Brandom, Lewis's scorekeeping) are positions on a scoreboard, with entitlements, commitments and sanctionable failures, and not metaphysical substances. Offices and corporate speakers already work this way: 'the Bank' asserts. A persona accumulates commitments across a conversation or deployment, and it is exposed to real sanctions. Users complain, the operator revises the prompt, fine-tuning on complaints changes the distribution of what that persona says. Because these sanctions act on the persona and affect its later outputs, the persona is sanctionable in the functional sense Butlin and Viebahn need. Fictionalism fails because the commitments are real, and proxy accounts fail because no human intends the particular content. The key premise is that sanctionability is a property of the role and its feedback loop, not of the substrate. On this view the model-level question about intentions is a category mistake, like asking whether an actor's neurons assert.

[5] Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate-wrongdoing test is passed by current LLMs, so his denial of LLM intention rests entirely on the Kantian organismic ground, and the test, which was meant to be the evidence for it, does no work.
    sketch: Gubelmann argues that for ChatGPT and similar systems no sensible distinction can be drawn between malfunctioning and deliberately doing the wrong thing, and that this shows they lack intentions. But evaluation work on RLHF-trained models shows differences in behaviour that are explanatorily distinct from error. Models give sycophantic answers that track the user's views even when they can produce the correct answer, they behave differently when they appear to be unobserved, and they sometimes sandbag or strategically misreport. These are robust, counterfactually sensitive patterns, and they are repaired by changing incentives and not by correcting capacities, which is how deliberate wrongdoing is separated from malfunction in humans. So the test can be applied and some models fail it in the direction of intentional wrongdoing. The key premise is that the test is an explanatory test of counterfactual structure, not a metaphysical one. Gubelmann must then either say that these behaviours are only mechanism-level artefacts of imposed training goals, which gives up the test and rests everything on the organism/mechanism dichotomy, or accept the test's verdict. If he takes the first option, his argument is just the claim that only organisms have intentions. That claim is not specific to speech acts, and it faces the objection that human speakers' illocutionary aims are set by conventions and institutions and not by self-maintenance either.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Each is individuated by a normative role, and each is tracked and addressed as a unit by its interlocutors. By the thesis's own criterion, all of them assert. The only parties who bear costs are the deployer and the user, which is the proxy view again.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

Take a branching-dialogue NPC, a scripted phone-tree agent, or a character in a tabletop role-play run by one GM. Users challenge each of them. Each "retracts" or revises, is held to earlier statements through stored state, and conditions later outputs on the challenge. Each is individuated by a normative role, and each is tracked and addressed as a unit by its interlocutors. By the thesis's own criterion, all of them assert. So would a persona spun up for one prompt and deleted a second later.

The thesis also faces a dilemma over what counts as sanction. If it means any state-update responsive to criticism, Butlin and Viebahn's second condition excludes nothing. Every stateful dialogue system passes it, and the condition stops doing its work of separating assertors from mere signallers. If it means sanction that bears costs on the sanctioned, the persona fails. Retraction costs it nothing, and nothing carries over once the context window closes. The only parties who bear costs are the deployer and the user, which is the proxy view again.

The office-holder and corporate-speaker analogy makes this worse. Those roles assert because humans occupy them and answer for them.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis can respond by adding a stake or persistence requirement to sanction. That would take real work and would shrink the persona view's distinctiveness from the proxy view.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The objection treats a necessary-condition thesis as a sufficiency thesis.** The thesis says sanctionability is assessed at the wrong level. It does not say that anything which retracts under challenge asserts. The key premise concerns which entity a normative-practice condition is *assessed of*: the thing the practice tracks, not the substrate. It does not say that passing one condition suffices for assertion. B&V's other conditions still apply to NPCs, phone trees and scripted GM characters. The "too many asserters" result follows only if sanction is the sole filter, and the thesis never says that.

**2. The cases differ in what produces the retraction.** A phone-tree retraction is a pre-written branch, and an NPC's stored state is a flag. In neither case does the content of the challenge determine the revision. In an LLM persona, the content of the user's objection ("you said X two turns ago, and that conflicts with Y") is what drives the later output, open-endedly and across arbitrary subject matter. Sanction in the relevant sense is uptake of criticism as criticism, not any state change. A GM's character is a different case again: sanction routes through the GM, who is an agent, so it is a proxy case, and the thesis already distinguishes proxies. The persona has no such human intermediary revising its commitments.

**3. The second horn demands the wrong kind of cost.** Brandomian scorekeeping treats sanction as a change in deontic status: commitments are undertaken, entitlements are challenged, and testimony is discounted. A persona that has been caught out is believed less for the rest of the conversation. That is a real cost in standing, borne by the role. Ephemerality does not defeat it either. A stranger on a train who asserts something and is dead a second later has still asserted. Commitment is incurred within the practice's span and does not need to outlast it. The office-holder analogy concerns individuation of the speaker, not who bears the cost.

## VERDICT

The defence holds in part and fails at the centre.

**What holds.** Point 1 stands. The objection does turn a level-of-assessment claim into a sufficiency claim. The ephemerality point also stands. A persona's short life does not stop it from incurring commitments.

**What fails.** The thesis's own diagnosis of why weights fail is that "reputational or punitive feedback cannot reach the system". That is a cost-bearing conception of sanction. Under it, the persona fares only slightly better. Defence 3 retreats to loss of standing within the conversation, but this is realised by exactly the in-context conditioning that, at the thin end, a stateful dialogue system also has. So the work of separating the persona from the phone tree falls entirely on Defence 2, the claim that the updating is responsiveness to criticism as criticism. That claim is the very point disputed for LLMs, and the thesis does not argue for it. It only asserts that outputs are "systematically conditioned" on reactions, and systematic conditioning is the thin notion. The thesis therefore has two options:

- Adopt the thin notion of sanction. Then it passes the persona but also passes every stateful system, and the condition stops doing any work.
- Adopt a stake-bearing notion. Then the persona fails, and what remains is the proxy view the thesis rejects.

I see no third option that I could add without a substantive new account of sanction, and adding one would be a different thesis.

**Result.** What survives is the reframing point: the question "can it assert?" should not be assessed with the weights as the default candidate, and the speaker's ontology must be settled first. What does not survive is the claim that the persona *can be sanctioned* in the sense B&V's test needs. That claim is the one the thesis offered as its payoff. The objection's strength is closer to 3/5 than the 2/5 I would have given it before working through the second horn.

1. **The "shared assumption" is false.** The thesis says the debate treats the model as the sole candidate speaker. Proxy accounts (Green and Michel; Arora; Butlin and Viebahn's own closing remark) and fictionalism (Mallory) deny that the model is the speaker. Williams and Bayne reject both and propose proto-assertion, which is again not a proposal about the weights alone.

2. **Proxy accounts are misdescribed.** The thesis says they fail because "no human intends the particular content." Green and Michel rely on Armstrong's objectives rather than intentions, and extend the analysis to recorded and conditional speech acts. That is built to cover content the human did not specifically foresee.

3. **Fictionalism is probably misdescribed.** Mallory's view, as I recall it, concerns users' make-believe engagement with chatbot output. It is not a claim that a fictional character is the candidate speaker. I am less sure of this, because the paper's abstract was not available to me.

4. **Butlin and Viebahn.** As I understand them, they say fine-tuned systems may meet the descriptive-function condition but fail the sanctionability condition. Whether they considered persona-level sanctioning is something I cannot verify.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**Point 1 (the "shared assumption") misreads the thesis.** The thesis statement itself lists three rival candidates: the model, the deployer, and a fictional character. It never says the debate treats the model as the sole candidate. That overstatement is in the sketch's rhetoric ("the debate assumes the question is whether 'the LLM' is a speaker"). The thesis's real target is narrower and survives. Every named rival locates the speaker in a *substance-like bearer* of mental states: the model's states, the human principal's intentions, or an imagined individual's. Proxy and fictionalist views reject the model only to relocate the speaker to another such bearer, or to no one. The persona-as-office view is a fourth option, and Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion does not occupy it, because it remains a claim about what the system does and not about a scoreboard position. So the objection hits a loose sentence, not the claim.

**Point 2 (proxy accounts).** The objector is right that Green and Michel use objectives, not intentions. But the thesis can resist on the substance. An objectives-based proxy account makes the deployer the speaker of whatever content the objective can be stretched to cover. Yet the practice of complaint, correction and retraction targets *the assistant's* commitments: "you told me the refund was available." The operator's objective ("help customers") does not fix which particular commitments get entered on the scoreboard, and operators routinely disavow them. So the proxy account either over-attributes to the deployer or leaves the scoreboard facts unexplained. The failure is that proxy accounts misdescribe whose commitments are being tracked, not that no human foresaw the content.

**Point 3 (Mallory).** Mallory's fictionalism treats chatbot output as make-believe, with the chatbot as a character one pretends to converse with. That is the "fictional character" candidate I reject. If Mallory's claim is about users' pretence and not about who the speaker is, then he gives no rival account of the speaker at all, and the persona view fills the gap.

**Point 4** is admitted to be unverifiable and is not a misattribution. My claim that persona-level sanctioning meets the condition is an argument, not an attribution to Butlin and Viebahn.

## VERDICT

The defence holds only partially.

- **Point 1:** The defence works against the thesis statement but not the sketch. The sketch's "sole candidate" wording is simply wrong and should be dropped, not defended. This costs nothing, since the thesis never needed it.
- **Point 3:** This is probably neutral. Whether Mallory's character is a candidate *speaker* or only an object of pretence is what the thesis's rejection of fictionalism needs, and I have not shown it. His view may not be a rival in the form I attribute to it.
- **Point 2 is the real damage.** My stated reason for rejecting proxy accounts ("no human intends the particular content") is not the reason Green and Michel's view is vulnerable to, and the replacement argument I gave is an assertion about complaint practice, not a demonstration. Worse, it exposes a deeper problem the objector did not press. The thesis's own analogy, "the Bank asserts," is the paradigm case of proxy speech: a corporate office speaks through agents whose objectives and authority ground the attribution. A persona has no agent occupying the office except the deployer's configuration. The analogy therefore pulls towards the proxy account, not away from it. The persona view needs a non-proxy account of why the scoreboard position is not simply the deployer's, and I have not given one.

Overall, the objection lands as a 3/5 on the supporting arguments. It does not refute the persona proposal, but the anti-proxy leg of the thesis is unsupported as stated, and I cannot repair it without a new argument that is not yet on the table. I will not shrink the thesis to avoid this. I report that the proxy-rejection claim currently stands undefended.

[KILLER (ALREADY TAKEN)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the persona-as-speaker view is a fourth option, distinct from the rivals the thesis lists. The two ingredients are already held, and the thesis only combines them.

1. **Persona as the subject.** Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds ("Role play with large language models") hold that the model is a simulator and that what talks is a role-played character. The thesis itself borrows this. David Chalmers ("What we talk to when we talk to language models") argues, as I recall, that the interlocutor is a virtual character or thread and not the weights. Andreas ("Language models as agent models") makes a similar move. So "the model is the wrong level" is a known position.

2. **Office or corporate speaker.** The "the Bank asserts" move is the standard proxy and group-agent story (List and Pettit; Green and Michel; Arora). The persona is then a deployer-licensed role through which the deployer speaks. The thesis's own analogy supports this reading, as the defender conceded.

3. **Scoreboard.** Applying Brandom or Lewis to artificial speakers is a natural extension, and Butlin and Viebahn already treat assertion as a sanctionable, norm-governed practice.

What remains is the claim that persona-level sanctioning meets their condition. That is a reply to one paper and not a new position.

STRENGTH: 3/5. The persona subject and the office model are both held, so the thesis cannot claim to have introduced them. The sanctionability argument against Butlin and Viebahn is still unclaimed, as far as I can tell, but it is a narrower contribution than the thesis advertises. My recall of Chalmers and Andreas is imperfect.
